copy.h1: When the problem is the door, not the lock
copy.lead: "Lift the handle harder" is not a repair. Most modern lock failures start inside the door — a worn gearbox, a dropped sash, keeps a millimetre out of line. Doorfix's eight branches, from Canterbury to York, specialise in exactly that hidden machinery, and fix it before it locks you out.

services.heading: Inside-the-door specialists
services.intro: Standard locksmithing is on the menu too — but this is the work that earns the name.
featured: Dropped, catching or slamming uPVC and composite doors realigned so the mechanism stops fighting the frame.
Multipoint gearboxes, follower springs and cams repaired or swapped — the failure everyone else calls 'a new door'.
Full mechanism strips and cylinder upgrades matched to your exact door profile, first visit.
Handle stopped lifting with the door shut? Our speciality. Non-destructive entry on multipoint doors is what we train for.
New cylinders and mechanisms fitted with the alignment set properly — the difference between 2 years and 15.
24/7 response, because a multipoint failure never picks a convenient evening.
The same mechanism-first approach for espagnolettes, shootbolts and window gearing.

about.heading: Why doors, specifically?
body: Around four in five modern lockouts aren't lock failures at all — they're door failures. The multipoint mechanism inside a uPVC or composite door is a strip of moving steel with a gearbox at its heart, and when the door drops even slightly, every lift of the handle grinds that gearbox toward failure. General locksmiths meet this mechanism occasionally. Doorfix branches meet it every working day.

That focus shows up in practical ways: our vans carry the gearboxes, keeps and repair strips that usually have to be ordered in; our engineers diagnose by feel which part of the strip has gone before the door is even open; and every job ends with the door re-aligned and toe-and-heeled — because a new gearbox in a dropped door is just a countdown to the next one.
There are {n} Doorfix branches, from Canterbury to York. Each runs its own diary on its own local number.
